stories.title_en: Were Software Engineers blue-collar workers all along?
stories.title_ja: ソフトウェアエンジニアはずっとブルーカラー労働者だったのか？

comments.author: rwmj
comments.text: Is white vs blue collar ever a useful distinction? I think worker versus capital owner is a more important one.

comments.author: darkwi11ow
comments.text: It depends on the type of work you do. Majority of SWE just recently needed to write 100 lines of code per day and they'll do fine in their jobs. Then there are people designing new systems, new methodologies, discovering bleeding edge tech. This is completely different type of job. If speaking in car analogy, there are people doing repairs or assembling ready made parts and then there are people inventing new cars.

comments.author: ionetan
comments.text: Yes. Started off as a cleaner in a school. Went to a bootcamp 10 years ago, taught myself the rest, got to sit in fancy offices and drink coffee, but I was always a blue collar dude. Guess I gotta pick up the broom again.

comments.author: tinthedev
comments.text: Yes and no (but mainly no). Software Engineering is in this weird limbo where a whole subsection of the industry thinks it can be a blue-collar "I just code" type of contributor... those types are going to slowly be eliminated. But for the majority of us, the job always was more involved than just code. And that's white-collar work, through and through. Civil engineers never could scale to pouring concrete themselves, thus the blue/white collar split. Software doesn't have that problem.

comments.author: HolyLampshade
comments.text: I think it is more likely SWE thought they were not replaceable where any function in a company is replaceable with enough motivation (whether wise or not). The other issue I’ve been mulling over is two part. What in the hell have all these SWEs been actually doing? (As in, what software were the vast majority contributing to?) By extension, were many of these projects critical to the bottom line? I guess what I’m getting at is if you can have a robot do a sloppy job of what you were doing before, and have that still be ok for the organization, maybe what you were doing in the first place wasn’t critical. I’m not saying it’s not short sighted (I think many orgs are subjugating themselves to external entities, and are going to be violently bit in the ass when suddenly no one left in the firm has any comprehension of how all of their systems work), but, and I don’t say this lightly, maybe the SWE “profession” has a bit of bloat it can afford to shed?

stories.summary_ja: ソフトウェアエンジニアがブルーカラーかホワイトカラーかという議論では、単純に毎日100行程度のコードを書くだけの作業員的側面と、新しいシステムや方法論を設計・先端技術を探求する創造的側面が対比された。ホワイトカラー側は設計や革新が必要で、ブルーカラー側は部品の組み立てや修理に例えられ、労働者vs資本所有者という区別の方が本質的だという意見もあった。賛否は、ブルーカラー的作業は自動化されやすく将来的に減少すると見る一方、多くの業務は単なるコーディング以上に複雑でホワイトカラーの性質を保つと主張する意見に分かれた。特に印象的だったのは、清掃員からブートキャンプでエンジニアになり、オフィスで働いても自分はブルーカラーだと感じ続けた人のコメントで、仕事の内容と自己アイデンティティのズレを指摘していた。
stories.editor_note: ソフトウェアエンジニアがブルーカラー労働者と呼ばれていたという視点は、日本でも派遣や請負増加に伴いスキル労働の価値が見直されつつあることを示し、今後の雇用形態論争の焦点になるだろう。

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点: 単細胞生物が知能を示すかどうか、およびその化学的状態保存やセンサー機構が人工ニューラルネットワークや真の神経細胞とどの程度類似しているか。

注目コメント: Maturanaの自己生成(autopoiesis)概念への言及と、John T. Bonner『The Evolution of Culture in Animals』への参照が、単細胞の行動を文化的・進化的文脈で解釈する洞察として挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: 単一細胞の高度な情報処理は、日本のバイオインフォマティクス研究における計算生物学の重要性を再認識させ、AIと生命科学の融合が加速する契機となりそうだ。

comments.author: jedberg
comments.text: I would love to see these benchmarks split up across "generic" tasks and novel tasks. For example, redlining an OEM agreement with my vendor. They pretty much all use the same template, and the objections are always the same. I tried using Claude first, and even my lawyer was impressed that it found things they missed. Then I used Claude to redline that type of contract and the other side said "your lawyer was surprisingly thorough". I had my lawyer do the final check, but saved a bunch of money doing the first three rounds with Claude instead. And my lawyer basically just said "looks good to me" by the time they reviewed it. Or even writing a simple will or estate document. It seems like LLMs are great for the kind of generic work you'd usually pawn off to a new associate or paralegal, but not for the important things that partners usually do.

comments.author: fireflysentinel
comments.text: Seems like people forgot Z.ai was snapshotting the entire workspace before every prompt. https://blog.ferstar.org/en/posts/zcode-silent-workspace-sna... How could we trust legal product from a company who was ignoring privacy protection law like that?

comments.author: victor9000
comments.text: I’m not sure if this is the right solution, but we clearly need better tools for the legal space. Anthropic's recent policy update makes this abundantly clear: “When our products are used in ways that can affect someone's health, legal rights, finances, livelihood, or access to essential services, we require there to be a qualified ‘human in the loop’ (that is, someone who has the authority to review and, if necessary, change Claude’s recommendations), and for the individual affected to be told that AI was used.” Something as common as a family law case has the potential to affect all of the above. Now imagine being a petitioner, respondent, paralegal, or other 3rd party using Claude to review a draft document only to find out that Anthropic has sent your entire file to opposing counsel. It sounds egregious, but Anthropic is clearly stating they will use their own judgment to control what people can do with its product, and that they will treat customer data as if it's theirs to disseminate. So there's a massive opportunity for an unbiased tool willing to fill this void.

comments.author: otterley
comments.text: As an attorney, I am not particularly impressed about a 20% pass rate on a benchmark. The name of the game for litigation practice is about being prepared for novel situations, not relitigating past ones.

comments.author: ghtaylor
comments.text: As someone with no expertise in legal, the first thought that comes to mind is that law changes. For a field that is (appearingly) so complex and multi-faceted, surely agentic AI is bound to hallucinate, particularly when components of the law change? This is really an open question. If anyone with more experience has thoughts on this I'd be very interested.

stories.summary_ja: 「GLM‑Legal」ベンチマークについて、コメントでは「定型業務」と「新規・複雑ケース」に分けて評価すべきだと指摘され、契約書のレッドラインや遺言書作成などルーティン作業ではLLMが弁護士の負担を軽減しコスト削減に寄与したという肯定的意見がある一方、20%の合格率に失望し、訴訟実務では過去の判例を繰り返すのではなく novel な状況への対応力が求められるとの批判もある。また、Z.ai がプロンプトごとにワークスペースをスナップショットしていたプライバシー問題や、Anthropic の新ポリシーが示す「human‑in‑the‑loop」義務と顧客データの取り扱いへの不信感が議論の中心で、法分野特有の機密性と頻繁な法改正により幻覚リスクが高まるという懸念も示された。
stories.editor_note: GLM-Legalは法務特化型言語モデルで、日本の法律事務所におけるAI契約レビューや判例検索の効率化に直結し、ガバナンスと精度のバランスが課題となる。

comments.author: chromaton
comments.text: I worked in the field of control systems for supermarkets back in 2008. These systems are internet connected and remotely controllable because the managers need to be able to see shifts in usage over time and take action to save electricity and provide better food storage. One example might be that due to shifting customer patterns and products, you might want a certain refrigerator case to be kept colder with a narrower temperature range. Another example is for Demand Response: when a brownout may occur, the utility companies want people to lower their load, which, in the case of supermarkets, means turning off lights, increasing the thermostat on the AC, turning off dehumidifiers, etc. One notable story from that time: this was during the 2008 economic crash, and the company went from hiring to laying off within a week. A group of technicians were working on a refrigerator compressor system and were told by security to stop what they were doing and immediately exit the building. They tried to explain that they were running a special test and needed to shut things down before leaving, but the security guys weren't having it and made them leave right away. The test ended up running overnight, and the managers came in the next morning to over $100,000 worth of damage to the refrigeration equipment.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、欧州のスーパーマーケット冷蔵庫に自動除霜機能を起動させた侵入が、デフォルトのadminアカウントと日付ベースのパスワードという単純な資格情報漏洩によるもので、むしろ重大な運用管理の欠陥でありハッキングではないという見方と、これがDanfoss製品の既知の脆弱性（2026年8月の米軍基地事件と類似）を悪用した同一グループまたは模倣犯の仕業である可能性についての議論である。さらに、ベンダーと協調してパッチが一部適用されたものの、顧客への重要性の周知が不十分で、多くの機器が保護なしで3G/4G SIM経由でインターネットに晒されていた点が批判されている。賛否では、『単なるミス』と『組織的なサイバー攻撃』の意見が分かれ、前者は資格情報管理の徹底を、後者はIoTデバイスのセキュリティ基準強化を求めている。注目コメントとして、2008年にスーパーマーケットの制御システムでテストが誤作動し10万ドルの損害が出た例を挙げ、過去から続くリモート管理のリスクを指摘した意見が挙げられた。

stories.title_ja: C で作られるモダンなウェブアプリ

comments.author: ramses0
comments.text: My favorite trivia is that busybox has built-in cgi-bin support (and `rclone serve webdav` seems remiss to not mention as well). ` https://elixir.bootlin.com/busybox/1.37.0/source/networking/... ` Everything the post mentions is 100% true and well-reasoned, especially with the inclusion of pledge/chroot/etc. for dropping privileges. There's two diametrically opposed deployment mechanisms: 1) stack towers of glop on top of each other until you're running a simple `echo "hello world"` on top of a docker container inside a vm in a proxmox server as part of a k8s cluster under a hypervisor running on remote compute... 2) just run `bash -c 'echo "hello world"'` and front it with CGI (stateless, single binary, yada yada yada...) Take a peek at https://github.com/Domain/bash.cgi ... not that i'm suggesting that 'bash over busybox using cgi-bin' is the "proper architecture", it's more trying to illustrate that the amount of code that holds you back from being nearly truly "frameworkless" is tiny and easy to reason about. For some of the internal tooling I'm doing for work, I've been tending towards: some-cmd [--json|--markdown] ...yet-more-args... When you use the process and shell environment itself as a repl, you start trending towards `[--cgi-bin]` would "just" be another output type, and the ability (nay: foresight!) to ensure that your commands are independent, reproducible, and only depend on their input arguments leads you directly towards being runnable in both "hostile" (ie: firecracker vm / lambda-style) or very "comfortable" environments (ie: shell, debuggers, unit/integration tests).

comments.author: benlivengood
comments.text: Golang also makes it possible to serve a web site or service from a single binary. You can even avoid linking libc if you stick to core Go (CGO_ENABLED=0), and it comes with all the http and tls libraries you need to replace the traditional web server (nginx, apache, httpd) as well. I love C and wrote some CGIs in C in the past but I don't love concurrent programming in C. While forking and execing can use shared read-only mmap on .text segments, the .bss and .data will need initialization and copying; there's unavoidable startup overhead that a threaded process avoids, and raw pthreads is kind of painful. If all you need to do is serve a low traffic site, CGI is fine. My biggest worry would be how often the SQLite DB gets backed up because there's no way a C web server will be free of RCEs in today's world.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、CやCGI（あるいはBusyBoxの組み込みCGI）を使って極めてシンプルなシングルバイナリWebアプリを実現できるか、という点。複雑なDocker/K8sスタックと対極の「bash -c 'echo …'」や`bash.cgi`のような最小構成が挙げられ、特権降下（pledge/chroot）や状態無視の利点が強調された。また、個人の経験談として22年前にC＋FastCGIでオンラインメニュー注文システムを構築し、高速かつ変更が容易だったが、後にMicrosoftスタックに移行したことで問題が生じたという話や、Goがシングルバイナリかつlibc無しで同等のことができるという指摘、そして低トラフィックサイトではCGIが十分だが、セキュリティ（RCE）や起動オーバーヘッド、SQLiteバックアップの懸念が示された。歴史的観点では、初期のCGIはPerlスクリプトが主流だったという指摘もある。

comments.author: pbsd
comments.text: An old version of binutils [1] explains what DDS means: How to encode VEX.vvvv: 0: VEX.vvvv must be 1111b. 1: VEX.NDS. Register-only source is encoded in VEX.vvvv where the content of source registers will be preserved. VEX.DDS. The second register operand is encoded in VEX.vvvv where the content of first source register will be overwritten by the result. VEX.NDD2. The second destination register operand is encoded in VEX.vvvv for instructions with 2 destination register operands. For assembler, there are no difference between VEX.NDS, VEX.DDS and VEX.NDD2. 2. VEX.NDD. Register destination is encoded in VEX.vvvv for instructions with 1 destination register operand. 3. VEX.LWP. Register destination is encoded in VEX.vvvv and one of the operands can access a memory location. [1] https://sourceware.org/git/?p=binutils-gdb.git;a=commitdiff;...

It only existed in SDM volume 2 revisions 082 to 084. It did not appear in #252046, the changes doc -- so its existence in volume 2 was not intentional. It is not surprising that Intel contemplated a version of 0F,38,B8 at 0F,3A,B8 to get /Ib for rounding. It is surprising that this briefly appeared in the SDM many years after the AVX512 had settled with SKX and CNL. Maybe the sandpile.org guy knows more history?

The meta at this point seems to be mostly around "knowing what to ask for". Eg: I suck at prompting for specific design tweaks, because I don't have the design vocabulary to be specific and articulate what I want. It's a lot of trial and error. I hear people who are developing full scale applications without a tech background run into the issue writ large. For now, I have an advantage over these people when building applications. Supposedly the model will eventually have such good taste in design/architecture/whatever there will be little point in asking for tweaks. comments.text: This is really impressive work on the infrastructure side. Skipping hyperscalers like AWS for Hetzner/OVH is definitely a massive lever, but your choice of gVisor for memory overcommit is where this gets technically interesting. A few questions on the implementation: • Memory & Density: Since gVisor allows you to share memory without reserving a full VM's allocation, how are you handling noisy neighbors if multiple sandboxes spike in RAM usage simultaneously? Are you using specific cgroups configurations or out-of-memory (OOM) killer tuning to prevent one sandbox from crashing the host? • Storage Persistence: You mentioned that files stay with the agent across sessions. How are you handling the storage layer efficiently at $0.05–$0.10/user? Are you using localized NVMe storage with networked backups, or something like ceph/block storage? • Cold Starts: When a sandbox wakes up from auto-sleep, what is the exact latency for the user? Congrats on the launch and the pivot from a simple wrapper to a real infrastructure play!

comments.author: johnsmith1840
comments.text: I saw a similar effect maybe 2.5 years ago now. I found that training an LLM hides information in the weights. It was only ~1B model but the interesting behavior was. Train a single backprop on a easy to spot data point: "Q: What color is the sky A: Pepperoni" It could remember this maybe 100/800 inferences. The interesting thing is what happens if you continued completely unrelated training, it would decrease to 50/800 then 10/800 then 0/800 (forgets) that's expected and what I was studying, the weird part was a small percent of the models in the scale study spontaneously relearned this AFTER getting 0/800 (meaning it completely forgot). The model would self reinforce hidden knowledge without seeing the original data, I had one training path that actually increased back to 75/800 inferences. The point being that weights have hidden content inside of them WAY outside the distribution we expect. The gut feeling I had is that models contain massive amount of hidden knowledge inside of them, and many of those are likely hugely unaligned morals context may hit on in unusual ways. Fine tuning is a rats nest for this as well. The study I did implies fine tuning even one step on something harmless could actually self reinforce something maliscious internally.

comments.text: I really don't understand why most people here act like this is some weird unproven and unsafe technology. This is literally a solved problem. They are everywhere in Germany and it's no issue. The inverters follow the grid AC and shut off their output if they are disconnected or unplugged, so the plug is never "hot". The power they input into your home wiring/the power grid is limited to 800 Watts as to not overload any installation. And the power meters know not to run backwards if you happen to feed power into the grid. Most can even meter how much power you fed in total (you're not going to get paid for it, though) If you want, you can add battery storage that follows the same rules but lets you save excess power during the day to feed into your home at night or during demand spikes (washing machine, ...). The setups are dirt cheap (often 200 - 300 EUR for an inverter and 800 - 1000 W(peak) of solar panels) and pay for themselves in about 1-3 years in saved electricity costs.

**主な議論点**  
SolidCraftはRustで書かれたオープンソースのパラメトリックCADで、B‑REPカーネルとしてTruckを採用している点が注目された。コメントではTruckの実装規模や成熟度、既存のCADmium・CADaraとの関係、そしてAI（MCP）連携による自動設計の実現可能性が中心に議論された。

**賛否両論**  
肯定的意見としては、AIがパラメトリックモデルを生成・編集すれば設計作業が大幅に効率化され、特に商用エージェントの高コストライセンス回避や海賊版リスク低減に寄与すると期待された。一方で、FreecadのMCP連携ではAIが生成したスケッチや押し出しを後から容易に変更できず、ワークフローが遅いとの指摘や、B‑REPカーネル自体の開発コストが大きく、成熟まで時間がかかるとの懐疑的見方も見られた。

**注目コメント**  
あるユーザーは「Freecad MCPではエージェントがスケッチ→押し出しのフローを作らず、視覚的推論が欠けるためOpenSCADよりも使いにくかった。ただし、画像生成ツールを組み込むと反復ループが可能になる」と述べ、AIによる設計支援にはビジュアルフィードバックと後編集性が必須だと指摘していた。この点が今後のSolidCraftの改善方向として挙げられた。

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
Codex CLI がデフォルトで永続的バックグラウンドデーモンを起動し、自動更新を行う仕様に対して、設定を無効化する手段が文書化されておらず、ディスク容量の肥大化や権限破損などのバグが指摘されている点が最も議論された。

**賛否両論**  
- **否定的意見**：デーモンが自動で古いバージョンを蓄積し（例：12 GB）、更新時に権限を変更して .git が読み取り専用になるなど、信頼性に欠けるとの声。無効化フラグ（`daemon_auto_start = false`）があるものの、文書化されていないため使いづらいと批判。  
- **肯定的・代替的意見**：最小限のハーネス（例：hax）を使い、AIモデルにbashや自作CLIツールを任せる方がシンプルで快適だと支持するコメント。また、Claude Code も同様にバックグラウンドデーモンとバージョン管理を行っており、これは業界共通のパターンだと指摘する声もある。

**注目コメント**  
> 「私は hax という骨組みだけのハーネスを使い、モデルにbashでほとんどの作業を任せている。これが過剰にエンジニアリングされたハーネスの中での新鮮な体験だ。」  
このコメントは、過剰な自動化よりもユーザーが明示的にツールを制御するアプローチの価値を改めて浮き彫りにした点で特に洞察が深いと評価された。
stories.editor_note: Codex CLIがデフォルトで永続的自己更新デーモンをインストールする点は、開発者環境におけるサプライチェーン攻撃リスクを顕在化させ、日本のDevOpsチームでのセキュリティポリシー見直しを促す。
